# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening form of systolic heart failure that emerges toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery in previously healthy women [1]. The first universally accepted definition was established by a National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) and Office of Rare Diseases workshop in 2000, which characterized PPCM as a rare cardiomyopathy of unknown cause occurring in the peripartum period in previously healthy women [2]. PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion in women presenting with heart failure and systolic dysfunction of unclear etiology; the 2010 ESC Working Group definition requires development of heart failure toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, and left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction generally below 45% [3]. The 2019 Heart Failure Association position statement reaffirmed this framework, characterizing PPCM as heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) in the last month of pregnancy or the months after delivery [4].

## Epidemiology and risk factors

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography and ethnicity. Worldwide, the estimated incidence is approximately 1 in 2,000 deliveries, ranging from about 1 in 300 in rural Haiti to 1 in 20,000 in Japan [5]. This variation is thought to reflect socioeconomic and genetic factors, and diagnosis is frequently delayed [6]. Incidence is higher in women of African ancestry and in those with older maternal age, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and multiple gestation pregnancies [1]. A nationwide US analysis documented temporal trends in incidence and outcomes [7], and pre-eclampsia is recognized as the strongest risk factor for the disease [8].

## Pathophysiology

A major conceptual advance came from murine work demonstrating a hormonal-vascular mechanism. Female mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Stat3 develop PPCM; treatment with bromocriptine, an inhibitor of prolactin secretion, prevents disease, while myocardial STAT3 protein is reduced and serum levels of activated cathepsin D and 16-kDa prolactin are elevated in patients [9]. The prevailing hypothesis holds that unbalanced peripartum oxidative stress triggers proteolytic cleavage of prolactin into a potent antiangiogenic, proapoptotic, and proinflammatory 16-kDa fragment [6]. The cause of PPCM is multifactorial, with environmental and genetic factors and pregnancy-associated conditions such as pre-eclampsia contributing, and animal studies implicate impaired vascular and metabolic function as central to disease development [8]. The disease is now understood in large part as a vascular disorder triggered by the hormonal milieu of late pregnancy [10].

## Genetics

PPCM shares a substantial genetic basis with dilated cardiomyopathy. Among 172 women with PPCM, 26 distinct rare truncating variants were identified in eight genes; the prevalence of truncating variants (15%) was significantly higher than in a reference population (4.7%) but similar to dilated cardiomyopathy cohorts, and two-thirds were in TTN [11]. A larger genetic and phenotypic study confirmed that approximately 10% of women with PPCM harbor truncating variants in TTN, and although such patients present with a lower ejection fraction, no significant differences in recovery rates were observed [12]. These findings underpin arguments for offering genetic testing, particularly in women with a positive family history [4].

## Clinical presentation and diagnosis

Symptoms of heart failure mimic those of normal pregnancy, often resulting in diagnostic delay, and echocardiography showing decreased myocardial function is essential for diagnosis [1]. Because dyspnea, fatigue, and leg edema are common in the peripartum period, a high index of suspicion is required; measurement of natriuretic peptides, electrocardiography, and echocardiography are recommended to diagnose or exclude PPCM, and key differential diagnoses include pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, and hypertensive heart disease [4]. Additional biomarkers and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may aid diagnosis and prognostication [13].

## Management

Medical therapy follows established HFrEF principles, with modifications to ensure fetal and neonatal safety, including avoidance of ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers during pregnancy [1]. Anticoagulation is considered given the elevated thromboembolic risk, and severe cases may require mechanical circulatory support or transplantation [13]. The prolactin-blockade hypothesis prompted clinical evaluation of bromocriptine: an antiangiogenic cleaved prolactin fragment is considered causal for PPCM, and experimental and early clinical observations suggested beneficial effects of bromocriptine [14]. A proof-of-concept South African trial reported favorable outcomes [15], and a German multicentre randomized study compared bromocriptine regimens added to standard therapy [16]. Nonetheless, the role of bromocriptine remains incompletely established and randomized trials remain necessary [1].

## Outcomes and prognosis

Outcomes are heterogeneous. In the prospective multicenter IPAC study, which enrolled and followed 100 women through one year postpartum, the disease remained a major cause of maternal morbidity and mortality [17]. The global ESC EORP registry, drawing on participants from 49 countries, characterized contemporary presentation and outcomes; just under half of deaths occurred within 30 days of diagnosis, and just under half of women experienced myocardial recovery within six months [18]. Mortality may reach up to 10%, with a high risk of relapse in subsequent pregnancies, yet many patients recover within 3 to 6 months [19].

## Subsequent pregnancy

Counseling on future pregnancy is critical. In a survey-based study of 44 women with prior PPCM who had 60 subsequent pregnancies, outcomes differed according to whether left ventricular function had normalized [20]. Risks of a subsequent pregnancy differ based on pre-conception recovery status, with higher risk in women with non-recovered myocardial function, in whom pregnancy should be discouraged [1]. A dedicated ESC risk-stratification position statement provides structured guidance for women with cardiomyopathy or heart failure planning pregnancy [21].

## Historical context, registries, and the persistent knowledge gaps

The natural course of PPCM was first systematically described decades ago [22], and pregnancy-associated presentations have been compared between early and late onset [23]. Contemporary worldwide registries [24] and German cohorts [25] have refined understanding of phenotype and outcome, while incidence and racial differences have been quantified in US populations [26]. Comprehensive contemporary reviews emphasize advances in biomarkers, genetics, targeted therapies, and multidisciplinary care [27], and prior US clinical characterizations remain foundational [28]. Earlier reviews and management summaries [29,30] also helped consolidate the diagnostic criteria still used today.

## Conclusion

PPCM remains a serious cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, complicated by diagnostic delay due to symptom overlap with normal pregnancy. Advances in understanding its vascular-hormonal and genetic underpinnings have clarified pathophysiology, but disease-specific therapies are still being validated. Early recognition, evidence-based heart-failure management adapted for pregnancy, multidisciplinary care, and careful counseling about subsequent pregnancies remain the cornerstones of practice.
